property_summary: For any caller and any recipient address k, a successful low-level call from C to k during withdraw leaves balances[k] unchanged in the reference (because withdraw reverts on failed send), whereas the mutant that ignores the call result can zero balances[k] even when the send failed (e.g., when the callee reverts).

For any caller and any target address k, when withdraw is invoked sending C.balances[k] to k, the reference contract always reverts if the low-level send to k fails (so balances[k] remains unchanged because the whole call reverts), whereas the mutant that ignores the send result can succeed while zeroing balances[k] even if the send to k failed (e.g., when k is a reverting contract).

For any caller and any recipient address k, calling withdraw either (A) fully reverts on failed low-level send so balances[k] is unchanged (reference), whereas the mutant can succeed while zeroing balances[k] when the callee reverts; thus the reference always preserves balances[k] when the external send to k fails, but the buggy variant may not.

After any call sequence where an address funds the contract and then calls withdraw, the reference contract ensures no other address's balances change due to reentrancy (balances(k) after withdraw equals balances(k) before withdraw for all k); the mutant removing the reentrancy lock allows a reentrant attacker to alter other addresses' balances during withdraw, violating this invariant for some inputs.

Invariant: calling withdraw must not change the stored balance of any other address (balances[target] after withdraw == balances[target] before) for any target address; removing the reentrancy lock allows a reentrant attacker to drain or modify other addresses' balances during withdraw, violating this invariant for some inputs.

For any attacker address A and victim address V with arbitrary deposits, a call to withdraw by A never decreases V's balance (balances(V) after withdraw >= balances(V) before) in the reference contract because reentrancy is prevented; removing the lock allows a reentrant attacker to reduce other addresses' balances during withdraw, violating this rule for some inputs.

Invariant: for any attacker address A and any target address T, after A calls withdraw (possibly via a reentrant helper), the stored balances[T] returned by the contract equals its value immediately before that withdraw; removing the reentrancy lock allows a reentrant attacker to change other addresses' balances during withdraw, breaking this equality for some inputs.

For any attacker address A and any victim address V and deposit amounts, when A calls withdraw the total contract balance decreases by exactly the amount withdrawn from A's own stored balance (i.e., address(c).balance after withdraw == address(c).balance before withdraw - old balances[A]); removing the reentrancy lock can let a reentrant attacker change other stored balances and drain extra funds so the total contract balance change no longer equals A's stored balance, violating this equality for some inputs.

For any caller and any deposited amount, after calling withdraw the caller's recorded balance in the contract becomes zero (reference) — the mutant that omits zeroing the balance can leave the stored balance non-zero allowing repeated withdrawals.

For any depositor address and deposit amount, after a successful withdraw call the contract's recorded balances[depositor] becomes zero (reference); the mutant that omits zeroing can leave balances[depositor] > 0 allowing repeated withdrawals.

For any depositor and any deposit amount, calling withdraw always succeeds (does not revert) on the reference contract because it uses a low-level call that can forward all gas and return a success flag; replacing that with transfer can revert when the recipient's fallback uses more than 2300 gas, so the mutant can make withdraw revert for some recipient contracts.

For every depositor and deposit amount, calling withdraw on the reference C never reverts (it always returns successfully because it uses a low-level call and checks its boolean), whereas the mutant using transfer can revert when the recipient's fallback/receive consumes >2300 gas — so the property: withdraw always completes successfully for any depositor/address receiver; the mutant violates this for some malicious receiver contracts.

For any depositor and deposit amount, after funding C via fallback and then calling withdraw from that depositor, the reference contract's withdraw call always returns (does not revert) and leaves c.balance == 0; the mutant using transfer can revert when the recipient's fallback consumes >2300 gas, thus causing c.balance to remain nonzero for some inputs.
